title: I just launched my first game on Steam. Most of its assets started with AI, then had to become an actual working game.
author: thewholeshelf
selftext:
Hi everyone! I'm Martin, a developer from Denmark, and I just released my first game on Steam.

It's a tongue-in-cheek game called "Fuck the Ocean". The premise is that a man steps in a puddle, gets his sock wet, and decides that all water on the Earth has to go. It's an incremental game where you start throwing sand by hand, then hire helpers and buy increasingly ridiculous equipment. There are garden gnome catapults. Nobody involved is handling the situation particularly well.

Since this is r/aigamedev, here's where AI actually fits into the development.

Most of the assets started with generative AI. I used Nano Banana for artwork. For audio, including music, character voices and sound effects I used Elevenlabs.

The 3D pipeline involved generating reference images, generating models from those references - some of them were through ChatGPT and the Blender MCP and others I went straight to Tripo3d, then taking them through cleanup, rigging and animation in Blender. Generated 2D artwork was also edited and reworked for the game in photoshop.

That meant there was a whole production process after generation: getting models into usable shape, making animations work, keeping assets consistent, and making sure the game could handle lots of equipment and workers on screen. A nice-looking individual model and a useful game asset are two different milestones.

I am a bit deaf, so for me the sounds and voices were fine, but I also had to end up creating a filter than removed AI artifacts, since a friend of mine said it had some noise artifacts.

There's also everything around the assets: progression, equipment balance, interface behaviour, sound timing, and making the increasingly absurd machinery feel satisfying to use. Those pieces still need to work together, however the assets were made. Here I made AI help me by running some simulations of how "passive", "semi-active" and "active" progress would be. But ultimately it came down to playing the games a lot of time myself to get a proper feeling for it.

I'm excited to finally have shipped something. Normally I'm a 80% done, new shiny project type of person, but AI really gives superpowers and helps me to tie up the last parts.

If you'd like to see how it all came together:  
[https://store.steampowered.com/app/1864730/](https://store.steampowered.com/app/1864730/)
